extra.message: The search parameter from request.args.get('search') (routes/account.py:27) is interpolated directly into a raw SQL fragment: text(f"text like '%{search_param}%'") passed to query().filter(). An attacker can break out of the LIKE literal and inject arbitrary SQL (e.g. search=' OR 1=1 -- or UNION-based extraction) to read or modify the entire SQLite database. Use parameterized queries instead.

In validate_token(), the registration code submitted via POST /signup (form.registration_code.data) is interpolated into an f-string SQL statement: text(f"""SELECT id, code FROM {RegistrationCode.__tablename__} WHERE code = '{code}'""") executed with session.execute(). This unauthenticated endpoint permits arbitrary SQL injection; the except OperationalError at lines 24-25 also silently swallows database errors, enabling blind injection. Use bound parameters.

The 404 error handler interpolates request.path (attacker-controlled URL path) into a string passed to render_template_string(), which compiles it as a Jinja2 template. A request to a path such as /{{7*7}} or /{{ config }} triggers server-side template injection; Jinja2 is not sandboxed here, so crafted expressions can access template globals and lead to remote code execution, with attacker-controlled content reflected on the 404 page.

The base64-encoded 'preferences' request cookie is passed to pickle.loads() in the before_request hook (routes/account.py:118), which runs on every request without authentication and without any integrity/MAC check. An attacker who crafts a malicious pickle payload (e.g. via __reduce__) in this cookie achieves arbitrary remote code execution in the server process. The related handlers pickle-serialize data into the same cookie at lines 105 and 127-128.

GET /accounts/<int:user_id>/notes returns notes filtered only by Note.user_id == user_id (routes/account.py:45-46) without verifying that user_id matches current_user.id. Any authenticated user can change the user_id in the URL and read every other user's notes, including private ones (e.g. the seeded private admin note).

cwe: CWE-639: Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key

extra.message: POST /notes/<note_id>/delete loads the note with session.get(Note, note_id) and deletes it (routes/notes.py:48) without checking that the note belongs to current_user. Any authenticated user can delete arbitrary notes owned by other users (integrity loss / destructive IDOR).

cwe: CWE-639: Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key

extra.message: update_account() copies all submitted form fields into the user object via current_user.__dict__.update(filtered_values) without an allowlist. AccountForm (forms/account_form.py:7) exposes an is_admin BooleanField, so any authenticated user can POST is_admin=on to /account and grant themselves administrator privileges (privilege escalation). The email can also be overwritten and the password changed (lines 83-89) without verifying the current password.

cwe: CWE-915: Improperly Controlled Modification of Dynamically-Determined Object Attributes

extra.message: download() calls urllib.request.urlopen(url) with the user-supplied URL from POST /account/image (routes/account.py:60-61) with no scheme, host, or allowlist validation. This enables SSRF: requests to internal network addresses (internal services, cloud metadata endpoints) can be made from the server, and because urlopen supports the file:// scheme, local files can be read — their base64 contents are stored as the profile image and rendered back to the requesting user.

The Flask secret key is hardcoded as the well-known string "super secret key". This key signs Flask session cookies, so anyone with access to the source can forge arbitrary session cookies and authenticate as any user, including the admin (flask_login stores the user id in the session), completely bypassing authentication.

The POST /account route lacks @login_required (compare the GET handler at routes/account.py:18-19 which has it). Unauthenticated requests reach the account-update logic that operates on current_user and attempts to persist it, whereas all other state-changing endpoints require authentication. This missing authentication check on a critical function allows unauthenticated invocation of account mutation logic.

cwe: CWE-306: Missing Authentication for Critical Function

extra.message: Note text is rendered with the Jinja |safe filter ({{ note.text | safe }}), which disables HTML escaping. Note content is fully user-controlled via POST /notes (rich text from CKEditor, routes/notes.py:25-32) and defaults to private=False, so it is displayed on /home to all users. Any user can store a

render_table(..., safe_columns=['text']) renders the 'text' column of notes as raw HTML without escaping. The table is populated from the /search query; combined with the SQL injection in the same route (routes/account.py:33), attacker-controlled content (e.g. via UNION SELECT) is rendered as HTML in the victim's browser.

render_table(..., safe_columns=['text']) renders note text as raw HTML without escaping on /accounts/<user_id>/notes. Because that endpoint is also vulnerable to IDOR (routes/account.py:41-48), another user's note text (arbitrary HTML/JavaScript) can be rendered in a victim's browser (stored XSS).

The profile image is set to the arbitrary content fetched from the user-supplied URL, and get_base64_image_blob() derives the MIME type solely from the URL extension (guess_type at utils/profile_image.py:13) without validating that the content is actually an image. The result is rendered in an <object data="data:...;base64,..."> tag at templates/base.html:61 and templates/home.html:36 (note authors' profile images are shown to all users on /home), so a URL ending in .svg serving an SVG containing script yields stored XSS via image/svg+xml executing in the object element.

Flask-WTF is installed (requirements.txt) but CSRFProtect is never initialized, and all forms derive from plain wtforms.Form (not FlaskForm), so no CSRF tokens are issued or validated. Every state-changing endpoint (POST /login, /signup, /notes, /notes/<id>/delete, /account, /account/image, /darkmode, /registration-codes) can be triggered by a cross-site request while the victim is logged in, enabling e.g. silent note deletion, account/password changes, admin-only registration-code generation, and privilege escalation via is_admin.

A static registration code 'a36e990b-0024-4d55-b74a-f8d7528e1764' is hardcoded in the seed data and inserted into the registration_code table on first run. Anyone who reads the repository can submit this committed code at POST /signup to self-register, defeating the registration-gate mechanism.

Default accounts are created from hardcoded credentials: user@evfa.com with password 'user' and admin@evfa.com with password 'admin' (is_admin=True). Anyone knowing these public values can log in at /login and obtain full administrator access (registration codes, private notes, etc.).

download() reads the entire response body of the attacker-supplied URL into memory (response.read()) with no size limit, and the result is stored unbounded into the profile_image BLOB (routes/account.py:60-63). An authenticated attacker can point the URL at an arbitrarily large resource to exhaust server memory/disk (denial of service).

response.set_cookie('preferences', ...) at routes/account.py:105 (and in after_request at routes/account.py:127-128) omits the Secure, HttpOnly, and SameSite attributes, and app.py defines no SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE/SESSION_COOKIE_SAMESITE configuration for the Flask session cookie. The cookie is readable by JavaScript, sent cross-site, and transmitted in cleartext (nginx terminates on port 80 with no TLS in conf/nginx.conf).

The SQLAlchemy engine is created with echo=True, which logs every executed SQL statement and its bound parameters to stdout/stderr. Queries contain user emails, bcrypt password hashes, note contents, and registration codes, so anyone with access to application logs (Docker/container log aggregation) can reconstruct sensitive database contents.

cwe: CWE-532: Insertion of Sensitive Information into Log File

extra.message: POST /signup flashes 'User already exists' when the submitted email is already registered (routes/signup.py:58-60), allowing an attacker holding any valid registration code to enumerate which email addresses have accounts through the observable response discrepancy.

cwe: CWE-200: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor
